records.toxicity_detail: RHS (the hybrid's own page, under its "Potentially harmful" heading) states: "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and, on its Pets line: "Pets: Fruit are ornamental; not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". The RHS entry names the fruit only, gives no symptom list, no severity rating and no named animal (neither cats nor dogs), so toxic_to_pets is left null. NC State's page for this hybrid carries no toxicity block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, and MoBot's page has no toxicity statement.
unknowns: name_note is null: NC State (its single-entry Common Name(s) list and its Description opener), MoBot (prose) and RHS (its plant-profile subtitle) all give Burkwood viburnum; no split. NC State writes the hybrid with an ASCII x, MoBot and RHS with the multiplication sign; all three treat it as a hybrid. is_houseplant is false: NC State frames it as a Perennial, Shrub for foundation, hedge or specimen use in garden soil (USDA zones 4a-8b), and no admissible source for this hybrid addresses indoor culture. The research record had left it null; set at landing because the catalog's landing gate requires a boolean.

toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity-type evidence is RHS's 'Potentially harmful' block (fruit not to be eaten, wear gloves when handling) and its Pets line, which names no cat or dog. NC State has no toxicity block for this hybrid. No symptom list or severity is published by any admissible source.

is_edible set false only on RHS's statement that the fruit is ornamental and not to be eaten; no source says the fruit is poisonous, and no source states any edible use. MoBot and NC State do not address eating.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source states a damage-onset temperature for this hybrid. NC State's USDA zones 4a-8b and MoBot's Zone 4 to 8 are hardiness ratings, and RHS gives only 'H6'. The Clemson HGIC page that mentions a 10 F foliage figure is a multi-species genus page and was not used. Day/night temperature fields are null.

Humidity, indoor light (foot-candles), direct_sun_hours_max (the only NC State hour figures are the site-wide light legend), fertilizer fields, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and the watering day-intervals are null: no admissible source for this hybrid supplies them for an in-ground shrub.

water_regime left null: MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium' is mid-scale, and its Culture prose and RHS 'Moist but well-drained' are soil descriptions, not a watering instruction. No source gives a watering schedule.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), both open-ended or closed-band readings, while RHS lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so no ceiling can be set from the Neutral band and the Acid band gives no floor.

soil_drainage is moderate on MoBot's 'average, medium moisture, well-drained soil' and RHS's 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained'. NC State gives only a bare 'Good Drainage' with no moisture tag. MoBot also says the plant 'Prefers moist loams, but tolerates a wide range of soils', and NC State's description says it is 'adaptable to a wide range of soils and pH types'.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State lists Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day) and Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours), mapped to full_sun and part_shade. MoBot ('full sun to part shade') and RHS ('Full sun, Partial shade') agree.

Size disagreement: NC State (anchor, its own page) gives Height 8-10 ft and Width 5-9 ft (96-120 and 60-108 in). MoBot prose says 8-10 ft tall and 5-7 ft wide (structured Spread 6.00 to 7.00 feet). RHS says Max Height 1.5-2.5 metres and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (59-98 in), with a description reading 'about 3m tall' and a 10-20 year Time to Maturity. The NC State figures were used.

RHS describes the foliage as evergreen to semi-evergreen and a 'large evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub', while MoBot and NC State call it deciduous (NC State also tags it semi-evergreen; evergreen only in zones 7 and 8). This is not a schema field.

attracts_pollinators is true from NC State's Attracts (butterflies), its 'pollinator plant' tag and its Pollinator Garden landscape theme; MoBot's Attracts line also lists butterflies. No pollination claim was taken from a bird-food or deer-resistance statement.

No dedicated page for this exact hybrid was found at hgic.clemson.edu (genus page only), edis/ask.ifas.ufl.edu, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu or fieldreport.caes.uga.edu, so only NC State, MoBot and RHS were used. plantfinder.mobot.org cannot be fetched by the repo's qc tool, so the MoBot quotes were read from a browser render of the page.

records.name_note: Sources split on the genus. NC State's page for this exact name has the H1 Berberis bealei and gives the former name Mahonia bealei in its Previously known as field. MoBot's dedicated page is headed Mahonia bealei and says it is synonymous with Berberis bealei. RHS runs the opposite direction: its plant profile has the H1 Mahonia bealei and lists Berberis bealei (with Mahonia japonica Bealei Group) in its Synonyms field. This record follows NC State's current name and MoBot's synonymy, so Mahonia bealei is recorded as the former name of the same species, not as a separate entry. Common names also split: NC State's single-entry Common Name(s) list and MoBot's Common Name line both give Leatherleaf Mahonia (2 of the 3 sources). RHS's plant-profile common name is Beal's mahonia, and MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose reads Beale's barberry or leatherleaf mahonia. NC State's often-confused-with module for this page names Berberis aquifolium, the species this catalog already lands as Oregon Grape under the name Mahonia aquifolium; this record is a different species. Also distinct from Leatherleaf (Chamaedaphne calyculata), already in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: Human-scoped hazard, not a cat/dog finding. NC State's Berberis bealei page carries a "Poisonous to Humans" block with Poison Severity: Low (heading scope is humans; the page also says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics."). Poison Symptoms: "Ingestion of the toxic parts can cause stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea." Poison Toxic Principle: Berberine, a benzylisoquinoline alkaloid. Poison Part (full list): Bark, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. NC State's Plant Type field has 3 values (Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub), shown separately from its Woody Plant Leaf Characteristics field (Broadleaf Evergreen). Its Landscape Problems tags are Invasive Species, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Children, Spines/Thorns, Weedy. Its Appendage field is Spines. The page's #poisonous if ingested tag is also present. NC State's separate Edibility field says: "Not poisonous, but berries contain berberine that can cause stomach upset, especially with children." This conflicts with its own Poisonous to Humans block, which lists Bark, Leaves, Roots and Sap/Juice but not the fruit. RHS (Potentially harmful field) says: "Berries are ornamental; not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling". So the sources disagree on scope: NC State's Poisonous to Humans block names Bark, Leaves, Roots and Sap/Juice, while RHS names the berries, and NC State's Edibility field also names the berries. MoBot's page has no toxicity statement. No admissible page names cats or dogs.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: none of the three admissible pages (NC State, MoBot, RHS) names cats or dogs. NC State's toxicity is scoped to humans (Poisonous to Humans block, Problem for Children tag) and RHS's Potentially harmful note names no animal.

is_edible set false only on RHS's statement that the berries are ornamental and not to be eaten, which sits under the Potentially harmful field with a gloves warning. NC State's Edibility field says the berries are not poisonous but contain berberine that can cause stomach upset, especially with children, while its Poisonous to Humans block lists Bark, Leaves, Roots and Sap/Juice. No admissible source says the berries are grown or used for food, and none describes them as sour, so no conditional food use is recorded. MoBot has no edibility or toxicity statement.

Invasive status as sourced: NC State's page says 'This plant is an invasive species in North Carolina' and that it 'has since become established in parts of the southeastern United States, including North Carolina where it is invasive.' MoBot says it 'has been introduced into the southeastern U.S. where it has escaped gardens and naturalized from Maryland and Virginia south to Alabama and Florida', and its Invasive row has only a link ('Where is this species invasive in the US?'). NC State also says it is not recommended for planting in landscapes. No admissible source on a dedicated page for this exact name gave a Southeast-wide invasive listing beyond these statements. Search hits from UF/IFAS, Clemson, PSU, UMD and UGA were genus-level, multi-species or alternatives-list pages, not dedicated pages, so they were not used.

Species check against Berberis japonica / Mahonia japonica: MoBot's page for this taxon says 'It is very similar to M. japonica (native to Taiwan).' RHS lists Mahonia japonica Bealei Group among the synonyms on this taxon's page. NC State's often-confused-with module for this page names Berberis aquifolium, not Berberis japonica. No dedicated page for japonica was read, so no contrast is drawn between the two.

RHS is not used for sun, size or hardiness conclusions beyond agreement: its Max Height 1-1.5 metres and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (about 39-59 and 59-98 inches) are UK garden figures and differ from NC State's and MoBot's 4-10 ft by 3-8 ft, so the NC State dimensions anchor the size fields. RHS's H5 rating is a UK hardiness code, not a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f stays null.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State (Dappled Sunlight, Deep shade, Partial Shade), MoBot (Part shade to full shade) and RHS's Position (Full shade, Partial shade) support part_shade and full_shade. MoBot adds that the plant 'tolerates full sun (albeit often with some bleaching of foliage colors), but only in the cooler northern parts of its growing range', a conditional tolerance aside, so full_sun and part_sun are not added. RHS's Cultivation line ('tolerant of sun if soil is not too dry') is Mahonia genus-level text shared with the Mahonia aquifolium (Oregon grape) page and is not species evidence. NC State's image captions 'Sunburn Leaf' and 'Sunburnt Form' also show sun damage. direct_sun_hours_max is null because NC State's 2-6 hour figure is its generic Light legend, not species prose.

water_regime left null: MoBot's structured Water field is 'Medium', which is mid-scale. No source gives a watering instruction. MoBot's 'Established plants tolerate some soil dryness and drought' is a tolerance trait, and NC State's drought-resistance tag is likewise a trait. Moist-but-well-drained appears only as a soil description, which is used for soil_drainage.
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State lists only Acid (<6.0), an open-ended band, and RHS lists Acid, Alkaline and Neutral as acceptable.

soil_base garden_bed is an in-ground shrub classification; the sources describe garden soil conditions and none gives a potting recipe. soil_drainage 'moderate' follows MoBot's moist, well-drained wording and RHS's structured Moisture field ('Moist but well-drained or Well-drained'); NC State's bare Good Drainage is consistent. RHS's Cultivation sentence ('Grow in humus-rich moist but well-drained soil...') is Mahonia genus-level text and is not cited.
Humidity, indoor light, temperature, fertilizer and watering-interval fields are null: no admissible page frames this in-ground shrub that way.

MoBot's www.missouribotanicalgarden.org URL redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org, which refused a normal certificate check from this sandbox, so the MoBot page was read with an unverified-certificate fetch. Its quotes are from rendered text and are unconfirmed by the cached verifier, which skips that host.

RHS name status, recorded here uncited: RHS's Mahonia bealei profile shows Name Status Correct, and the same profile served at its Berberis bealei address shows Name Status Synonym. A bare one-word Name Status value evidences nothing alone and a label+value join is barred, so those citations were dropped at landing; RHS's direction is cited instead through its H1 (Mahonia bealei) and its Synonyms field (Berberis bealei). The accepted name follows NC State's current page name and MoBot's synonymy statement.

is_houseplant is false: NC State frames it as a Perennial, Shrub in USDA zones 7a-9b and an invasive landscape escape, and no admissible source addresses indoor use. The research record had left it null; set at landing because the catalog's landing gate requires a boolean.

records.name_note: Admissible sources agree on the binomial and on 'Japanese plum yew' as the lead name; they do not split. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list carries four alphabetized entries (Japanese Plum Yew, Japanese Plum-Yew, Spreading Plum Yew, Spreading Plum-Yew), and its first entry matches the common name used here. Missouri Botanical Garden renders a single Common Name line reading Japanese plum yew, and its Noteworthy Characteristics prose adds that the plant is 'commonly called plum yew'. RHS shows Japanese plum yew as the plant-profile common name beneath the H1 and lists 'cow's tail pine, plum yew' under Other common names. MoBot's prose and RHS's Other common names also apply the shorter name 'plum yew' to this species; this record is Cephalotaxus harringtonia only.
records.toxicity_detail: Admissible sources address toxicity to humans only; none names cats or dogs, so toxic_to_pets is left null. NC State's page for this exact name carries a human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' block and a header tag reading 'This plant has medium severity poison characteristics.' (Poison Severity: Medium, from the Poisonous to Humans block; the page carries no separate Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags). Its Poison Symptoms text reads: 'All plants in this botanical group are quite poisonous if ingested but are not dangerous to handle. Nervousness, trembling, slow pulse, pupil dilation, difficult breathing, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, convulsions; seizures, sudden death from acute heart failure if eaten in quantity.' NC State's Poison Toxic Principle field reads 'Alkaloid taxine, Volatile oil' (this is the source's own wording on its Cephalotaxus page, not carried over from Taxus). Poison Part: Bark, Leaves, Seeds. The same block says Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes, which sits beside its 'not dangerous to handle' sentence, so the handling guidance is mixed. NC State's description adds that the seeds and foliage of all plants in this botanical group are generally quite poisonous if ingested, and that the plum-like seeds are not edible; its Edibility field reads 'Not edible. Potentially toxic.' Missouri Botanical Garden disagrees on the fruit: its Noteworthy Characteristics says 'Female flowers produce fleshy, edible, plum-like fruits (to 1" long).' with no preparation conditions, and says nothing about toxicity. The two admissible sources therefore conflict on edibility, and is_edible is left null.

Pets (dogs, cats): harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". RHS lists no poison-part list and no symptom list. NC State's page has no Poison block for this species, no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags and no sap or skin-irritation warning; it lists Appendage: Spines, Problems: Spines/Thorns, and describes the leaves as having toothed margins and a dark terminal spine. NC State Plant Type tags (stacked, in order): Edible, Perennial, Succulent. Edibility scope differs between sources: NC State says "The leaves and stalk are edible" (human edibility, with no preparation instructions given), while RHS says the plant is harmful if eaten by dogs and cats; the sources do not address each other's scope.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's dedicated page lists its Common Name(s) as Autumn Rain-lily, Fairy Lily, Peruvian Swamp-lily, Rain Lily and Zephyr Flower, led by Autumn Rain-lily, but its Description prose opens with Rain Lily. RHS's dedicated page subtitle is Peruvian swamp lily. Rain Lily was chosen because NC State's Description prose opens with it and it appears in NC State's Common Name(s) list; Autumn Rain-lily and Peruvian swamp lily are the alternates.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS's dedicated Zephyranthes candida page carries a Potentially harmful row reading 'Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling' (handling warning kept). Its separate Pets row reads 'Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers' and names no animal, so it is not scoped to cats or dogs. RHS gives no symptom list and no poison-part list. NC State's page for this species carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags.
records.cool_rest_note: NC State: in containers, move the plants indoors to a cool but frost free area and give just enough moisture to keep the soil from drying out totally (a winter-storage instruction for container plants, not a rest cue for growing plants).
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only admissible toxicity evidence is RHS's unscoped 'Pets' row (names no animal) and a UGA/CAES 'Poisonous Plants in the Landscape' PDF (C-957) genus-level entry for Zephyranthes spp. listing all parts with symptoms ending 'fatal to livestock', which is livestock-scoped, genus/multi-species, and not cited here. No admissible page names cats or dogs for this species.
NC State's page for this species has no Poison block, no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags and no Attracts field, so attracts_pollinators is null. No admissible source names pollinators for this species.
is_edible false rests on RHS's 'not to be eaten' wording for ornamental bulbs; no source describes any edible use.

water_regime left null: NC State's only moisture wording for this species is about winter storage (kept cool and dry; containers given just enough moisture to keep soil from drying out totally), not a growing-season watering statement. Its tags list both 'wet soils tolerant' and 'drought tolerant'. RHS gives 'moist but well-drained'. UF/IFAS FP621 is a Zephyranthes spp. genus page (alternately wet and dry) and was not used.
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), all open-ended or all-inclusive, and RHS lists acid, alkaline and neutral as acceptable.

Soil drainage: NC State lists Good Drainage with Moist, and RHS's Cultivation text on this species' page says 'moist but well-drained soil' and 'Protect from winter wet', so moderate. NC State also tags wet soils tolerant, but there is no root-rot warning and no source asks for consistently wet soil.

Light: NC State's structured Light field lists full sun and partial shade (2-6 hours direct sun) and its prose says full sun gives the best performance; RHS lists Full sun. direct_sun_hours_max left null because no species prose gives an hour ceiling.

NC State Plant Type lists Annual, Bulb and Perennial (three values); the page also tags it semi-evergreen and evergreen, while RHS says deciduous. RHS Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres and Max Spread 0-0.1 metre were not used for size because NC State's own Dimensions block is the anchor.

MoBot Plant Finder (kempercode=c747) and ask.ifas/edis could not be read from this sandbox, so no MoBot content is used. UF/IFAS FP621 is genus-level and not used. No admissible source states fertilizer, humidity, temperature-damage or indoor light data for this species.
NC State is a different page from Zephyranthes atamasco and from the landed Lycoris pages; none of their content was used.
